utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, I'd first like to establish whether the videolink is functioning well. Could the representative of the Registry at the other side, the Moscow side, of the videolink confirm that he can hear us and that he can see us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the representative is speaking, but I don't hear him. We can see you but we can't hear you. Is the microphone switched on at the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, good morning, Your Honours. I hope you can hear and see us clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we now not only can see you, but we also can hear you. Before we continue the cross-examination of the witness, I'd like to move into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll take a break of five minutes to try to resolve a certain matter. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have resolved the technical problem, but we still have to go into private session for most likely only a few minutes again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about my comments to the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If any questions will be put to you about the memorandum, then you may answer them. At this moment, the Chamber was focusing on whether it could be made public and nothing else for the time being. Before we continue to hear your testimony, I'd like to briefly deal with a remaining issue. On the 15th of June of this year, P7840 was marked for identification pending agreement between the parties as to what portion of the document was to be tendered. On the 9th of August, the Prosecution advised that it had reached an agreement with the Defence to tender the document as currently uploaded in e-court under Rule 65 ter number 33827. That same day, the Defence advised that it does not oppose the document's admission into evidence. And the Chamber instructs the Registry to assign Exhibit Number P7840 to the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 33827 and admits it into evidence. Mr. Demurenko, in a few seconds, I'll invite the Prosecution to continue its cross-examination. But before I do so, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by your solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Finally, may I remind the parties that the parties are invited to seek agreement on the distance between the point of impact and the -- where the suggested line of firing would cross the Pale-Lukavica road. I think we have not heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, you have not. The last time the witness was here, I checked with certain staff members on our team that have better knowledge of the scenario and there are apparently two roads at issue, one being further along and one being closer. And so we were not able to reach -- I did talk with one of the members of the Prosecution as to that issue after having that discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if there are two roads but you could agree on the one and the other as far as distances are concerned, and then the Chamber will further consider how to understand the testimony considering the distance you agreed upon for both of the roads. Although it's my recollection that the Pale-Lukavica road was a road very, very often mentioned and I think always referring to one, that is, the shortest road, but perhaps we could even ask the witness further about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry we didn't make progress on that. A variety of circumstances may explain it, but I'm happy to meet with Mr. Ivetic at the first break. We have a couple of documents that we consider makes the issue easier to resolve and we'll see if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There was -- by the way, there was another matter, Mr. Ivetic. I think you announced there would be a preliminary matter to be raised and I think our information is that it could be done in the presence of the witness. If it has to be done now, you have an opportunity to do so. If you can do it later, then, of course, we would not bother the witness with it in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it does need to be done now so that if the issue does arise during the cross-examination, Your Honours already have the information and have had time to think about it. It relates to a -- there's a microphone open on the other side. The issue relates to four new documents that late yesterday, just before 4 p.m., the Prosecution gave notice of these four new documents for use in cross. They are 65 ter numbers 33830, 33831, 33832, and 33833. And at that time they were not released and available to the Defence in e-court until sometime after 4 p.m. Given that the cross of this witness started two months ago, in June, cross documents were to be given to the Defence at that time in June. These four were not among those notified to the Defence at that time. The Defence were further advised that all documents to be used with the witness for today's videolink had to be ready and given to the Registry last week, I believe by Thursday. Thus, we were quite surprised, under these circumstances, to only receive new documents late yesterday instead of at any of the prior occasions when such documents were due to be given. We would thus ask for a ruling from this Chamber in relation to this untimely disclosure if the Prosecution actually does seek to use any of the documents that they have given notice of potentially using with the witness. And that would be the submission of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Tieger, I leave it in your hands whether you want to respond now or whether you want to wait how cross-examination develops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Probably better to respond now, although part of my response implicates some -- at least one issue that I wouldn't want to share with the witness at this point, so if there is any way of doing that technically I would prefer to do so. Otherwise I'll try to speak more elliptically, whatever the Court chooses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the technicians can mute the videolink which means that Mr. Demurenko will not hear anything. At the same time, the representative of the Registry will not hear anything perhaps either, but that's perhaps acceptable as long as we're not hearing the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In essence, this is a bit of a tempest in a teapot for several reasons. First of all, of the exhibits that were mentioned, those four exhibits, two of them contain information that the Defence has long had. One is stills of the video of Mr. Demurenko on the 2nd of September that's already in evidence and that was displayed in several cases before. The second one is an exhibit list from the Karadzic case, the case from which the amalgamated statement tendered by the Defence was produced, and the -- of course, the transcripts of those proceedings and the amalgamated statement that all the information contained in there, including the actual live action tendering of the exhibits was -- was available too. The other two items are, in fact, two photographic depictions that I intended to use to discuss with Mr. Ivetic in connection with the Court's inquiry about the distance of the Pale-Lukavica road from the point of impact. I didn't -- I don't at this time have any intention to use them in the examination, so perhaps that puts the entire issue to rest. Beyond that, this is -- the assertion that this is untimely is the invocation of a rule that doesn't really exist. We provided these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read screen. There was some observation by the interpreters, I think, about speaking into the microphone or speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, happy to do that. The documents have been provided before the time they are being used. I can't recall a single time in my time in the Tribunal when there's been any attempt by an opposing party to block the admission of a document proposed to be used in cross-examination because of its so-called untimely submission. Indeed, I've never heard of it even when the documents were not on the list. In fact, what would typically happen is that people would note that they weren't on the list, ask for more understanding from the other side because it made following the examination much easier and the parties moved on. So I would say there's no -- and that certainly has to be the case when we're talking about two documents that simply contain a permutation of information already available to the other side. So there's no basis for an assertion that these documents should not be used by the Prosecution. That would be true of the two photographs at 33832 and 338333 if we propose to use them, but it's certainly true of documents which are only another form of the information which the Defence has long had. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I still have not heard from Mr. Tieger any explanation for why these documents were disclosed to us two months after all the other cross documents for this witness. That's first. And second -- I'm still talking. As second, to say the Defence has these documents, we have hundreds of thousands of other documents, the guidance of the Chamber and the procedure in this Chamber for notification of documents for cross, as Your Honours have multiple times referenced, is to give notice to the other side of particularly the set of documents that are going to be used with a witness. That is the purpose of it. To say that, yes, in one of four expert reports, each of which is over a hundred pages long, none of which were prepared by this witness or identified this witness, that a single page from that multiple hundred-page report might be used with the witness is surely something that the Prosecution knew about earlier and had an obligation to advise the Defence of so that we could just prepare for any additional efforts that we have to undertake to try to prepare for redirect examination. And to say that the Defence has something, yes, but they disclosed millions of documents to us, but I dare say -- and if that -- if their position is that that is in compliance with their understanding of this Court's ruling as to cross document lists and when they should be provided and what should be on them, then I would ask for Your Honours to rule on that, if that is the Prosecution's submission, because I think it is wholly at odds with the way that we have conducted this trial for the past several years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, one question, are you suggesting that a still from a video which is already in evidence, if I understand Mr. Tieger well, that we should look then at the video, stop it at the relevant portion, rather than to use the still already prepared for practical purposes, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my position is that the still obviously was known to the Prosecution earlier and should have been disclosed earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not my question. My question is whether you suggest that this Chamber should rule that the still cannot be used but that, of course, what is in evidence can be shown to the witness and can be -- and that we then look at the video, stop at the time slot where the still is, and you would oppose for practical purposes to use the still rather than to -- and that you would not have any objection against playing the video, stopping it at a certain point in time, and then look at exactly the same what is shown in the still?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't have objection as to stills being used in lieu of video. The problem is with stills, when the Defence has wanted to use stills, we've had to disclose them to the Prosecution at an earlier time period so everyone knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the video --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the other two documents are the ones that I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the video is still in evidence, then every single split-second of that video is evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether you play the video and stop it, or whether you have extracted the still from the video. Would you suggest that that's the appropriate way of dealing with the matter; that is, to just play the video and say, Stop at 43 seconds point 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we're arguing over semantics. Either is, I think, an acceptable method, either to play the video and stop it or to use a still. The issue is the timing of disclosure and it's more in relation to the other two documents that are not video stills.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The other two documents, I do understand, Mr. Tieger announced that he does not necessarily need to use them to the witness -- with the witness. What we'll do is we'll wait until any of these documents comes up and then decide on that particular moment whether or not Mr. Tieger is using the documents rightly or that the late notification is opposing the use of the document. Therefore, could I invite the Registry, the representative of the Registry in Moscow, and Mr. Demurenko to put on their earphones again. Then, Mr. Tieger, if you are ready to continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Tieger, if you are ready to continue your cross-examination you're invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, when we concluded at the end of the day on the 15th of June, I had been about to present a number of photographs that were taken, but rather than simply doing that now, I think it's -- it will be more fair if I recap slightly where we were at the time so that you can understand the nature of those photographs, if you don't recall what had transpired at the end of the last session in court. We had been discussing, in part, paragraph 123 of your statement in which you refer to the terrain east of the direction of your investigation and noted at the end of that paragraph that that terrain was rocky and full of slopes, therefore not suitable for the mortars and said this would apply to bearings less than 170 degrees. So we had discussed that. And then I showed you a satellite photo of the Trebevic area which you had already seen previously in the Milosevic case. That's P2380.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it's good to show it to the witness once again. And display it to the Court as well, please. That's in tab 10 of the Registry's binder, but I think Mr. Doraiswamy is able to identify those items by the chronology of the P numbers or 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have it on my screen --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yet. Although I see that others in this courtroom have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a little technical problem for us. The document is available in Moscow?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P2380 now appears to be available to everyone in the courtroom and to you as well, Colonel. As you can see, and as I mentioned on the 15th of June, it depicts three areas, three way points, to the east of the 170 degree line, that's way point 5, 10, and 6. And I -- those way points are represented, in part, by photographs that were taken earlier and that are reflected in part in the ERN chronology in P2382 indicating the ERN ranges of the photographs that were taken for the various way points. And now I'd like to call up P19792 to look at some of the photographs of the area -- did I say P? 65 ter 19792. So that we can look at the photographs of portions of the areas east of 170 degrees. And if we could look first at page 38 of 19792, that depicts a portion of the terrain at way point 5. Next, page 39, e-court page 39, which is ERN 06197174. And next, page 40, the very next page, also depicting a portion of the area in -- at way point 5. Next looking at way point 6, if we could turn to page 47 in the e-court, and page 50. And finally turning to way point 10, if we could look at page 90 of 65 ter 19792. Page 92, please, and page 93. Having now had a chance to see some of the area, some of the terrain east of 170, Colonel, it is incorrect to say that the area east of 170 is "rocky and full of slopes and therefore not suitable for mortars." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. First of all, I never claimed that this territory is 100 per cent unsuitable for setting up a mortar. You will not find that in my evidence. I said that many spots are of that kind. Second, these photographs have nothing to do with the investigation because as you see, this film was made 12 years - 12 years - after the event. During that time, new roads could have been built, all roads could have been destroyed. Lots could have changed. These photographs have nothing to do, no relation to my investigation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you have your statement in front of you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Mr. Tieger, we have two pages of the statement, pages 13 and 14, that's been provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, I will read to you the pertinent portion of paragraph 123 of your statement: "I would also like to emphasise that the terrain east of the direction of my investigation, east of 170 plus or minus 5 degrees, was rocky and full of slopes, therefore not suitable for the mortars. This would apply to bearings less than 170 degrees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Tieger, your quotation started at: "I would also like to emphasise ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and it ends with "less than 170 degrees."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And on 15th of June, 2016, you confirmed to the Court that you did not test the area that -- that particular area east of 170 as you did the parts that you considered to be part of the investigation. And that's found at T 44193. So, Colonel, the fact is you did not assert that the area east of 170 had been -- contained many areas or a number of areas suitable for the placement of mortars but that you had somehow examined and excluded them. You claimed categorically that that area was rocky and full of slopes and unsuitable for mortars and you'd hadn't investigated it. That's the truth of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I want to say, once again, that the sequence of the investigation was as follows. We took the bearing from the possible point of impact and following the line presented by the French or English experts – I don't know who was there – drawn on the sketch, we checked, going over these points with our own feet, with still cameras. That's what it was about: that we established that the BE /unclear acronym/ was not true. Now, as to what was true - that's something that other people were supposed to investigate, instead of making a statement 2 hours after the explosion. We were doing our investigation several hours after the explosion. Now, 12 years after the event, these photographs have absolutely no relation to our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender P19792, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not a P number, it's a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, 65 ter 19792. Getting ahead of myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that the document in e-court appears to be 104 pages of which we've seen --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those -- I misspoke. Of course, those pages of P19792 that were shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll upload that extract.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That resolves my issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then 65 ter 19792, although I take it to be uploaded with a small a attached to it, will receive, Madam Registrar, what exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7843, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7843 and -- once uploaded is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you sought authorisation or permission from the VRS to go to the areas that you looked at in -- on the -- during your investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could call up, please, 65 ter 1D03888. That's at tab 13 of the Registrar's binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a document you've seen before during the course of the Karadzic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there an English translation available?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, there is. It was a recently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we see that side by side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a document dated 29th of August, 1995. It's from the security and intelligence department of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the Main Staff of the VRS. And it reflects the receipt of information that you disagreed with the assessment of UNPROFOR, requested information from the VRS to personally visit the location which UNPROFOR assessed as the point from which the shell was fired, the proposal by the signator of the document, Marko Lugonja, that you be given permission to visit the location after you marked the place where you will visit. And then it continues: "He also requested to visit hospitals where those who were wounded in the shelling in Blazuj on 28 August are being treated." That reference, Colonel, to the shelling in Blazuj is a reference to the shelling of a Serb area on the outskirts of Ilidza; correct? Colonel, do you recall your request to visit hospitals where those who were wounded in the shelling in Blazuj on the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are --

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited many places where people were wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the contents of this document, are you aware that Blazuj was a Serb-held area and the victims of that shelling would have been Serb? I saw a gesture. I don't know if there was an audible response, but I didn't hear one.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What is the question? Is the question whether I visited hospitals where wounded people were lying? Yes, I did. If you want to ask something else, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It should be clear that wasn't the question. The document refers to your request to visit hospitals where those who were wounded in the shelling in Blazuj on the 28th of August were being treated. So I asked for clarification purposes with reference to this document whether you could confirm that Blazuj was a Serb area and victims of a shelling in Blazuj would be a reference to Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that case specifically that you're asking me about, I don't remember. But I know for a fact that I visited all the places where shelling had taken place, including hospitals. That was one of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I don't quite understand the sentence to necessarily mean that the people who were injured in Blazuj. They're hospitalised in Blazuj. They were injured in an incident of shelling of the 28th of August. Do I understand you to suggest that the injuries -- that the shelling was on Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree there's a potential ambiguity there, but, yes, I understood that to be based both on the syntax of the sentence and some independent review that it refers to the shelling rather than the location of the hospitalisation. That's how I understood it. But that's why -- in part why I was seeking confirmation from this witness of his understanding before moving on to the rest of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could we then perhaps take it step by step. Mr. Demurenko, was Blazuj a Serb -- was that in Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember now, but I'm prepared to trust the document that's before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it was a question by Mr. Tieger, not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we're getting a little short of time so I'll move on to the next page before we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but perhaps we -- can you do that in a couple of minutes, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we would have to take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed and we'll take the break then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn the page in English, please. I would note that we had submitted a revised translation from CLSS to the Defence. They agreed to upload it. It apparently has not been uploaded. I will read instead the English translation from the revised document that both parties agree should have been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The document by Colonel Lugonja continues, Colonel, saying: "I propose granting him permission for this too. Demurenko wants in this manner to dissuade the UNPROFOR command that" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Persuade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm reading from the revised document, Your Honour. That's -- and the reason for the revision is that it contains a double negative that makes it hard to understand and I think CLSS tried to untangle that a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you start reading that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Again, starting the last -- the second page of the document in English in the last sentence of the document: "I propose granting him permission" -- last two sentences, excuse me. "I propose granting him permission for this too. Demurenko wants in this manner to dissuade the UNPROFOR command that the Serbs fired the shell and that they were not targeted."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Colonel, what Colonel Lugonja is referring to here are the two portions of the request by you that he noted early; that is, the request to visit the location where it was assessed that the shell was fired, and, two, to visit victims of the shelling on the 28th, the Serb victims of shelling on the 28th. And so he says that he -- he alludes to that by saying: Demurenko wants to dissuade UNPROFOR that the Serbs fired the shell on Markale, and, two, wants to dissuade UNPROFOR from the position that the Serbs too were not targeted during that period of time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will object to the question if he is asking Colonel Demurenko what Colonel Lugonja was trying to do without establishing foundation for how Colonel Demurenko would know what Colonel Lugonja had on his mind when drafting this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read it. Well, it's what the text alludes to, alludes to as what Mr. Demurenko would have said and that's a proper question to put to the witness. Perhaps you repeat the question, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, do you understand this as -- these last two sentences as referring to your two-fold request: One, to visit the location where -- from which you assessed the Markale II shell had been fired; and, two, to visit the victims, the Serb victims of the shelling in Blazuj? That's the first question. Is that how you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it in the following way. First of all, your sentence said that I asked for a permission. That's not true. I could not ask for permission, neither from the Serb nor the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, can I stop --

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the -- as for the sequence of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Somebody keeps typing while the witness is speaking and audibility is zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know who the -- well, I see one face expressing some feeling of guilt and the typing stopped, which is highly appreciated. Could you continue your answer, Mr. Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, the word "permission" is out of place completely. I could not ask for permission in view of my duties, neither from the Serb side nor the Bosnian side. They were not my bosses. They were not my superiors. If we are speaking about establishing contact with them to get them not to shoot at my personnel, then, in that case, yes, I did write various communications to them but they are not called "permissions." Without their permission, I was available to visit whatever I wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following question. You now explained what you brought to their attention, that you would rather not be shot at. Let's take it step by step. Did you ask this in relation to visiting a potential firing position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- every time. Communications were made in writing and sometimes phone calls were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm focusing exclusively on the document which is before us. Did you at that point in time make any submission that you wanted to visit a potential position of firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As part of the investigation, I needed to visit both sides of the front line with my assistants, both the Bosniaks and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you raise the matter of visiting the hospital in Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said I can't remember. I don't think I had been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no record, no evidence of my visiting that hospital, although I visited many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question is: Whether the reasons reported for your requests, whether you remember that you gave those reasons in your communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that is correct. Because to the question "why do you need this" asked by the Serbs about my visiting the Serb side, I could have answered: in order to either confirm or to refute the statement that was made 2 hours after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less than two hours after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reasons you are now giving are not exactly the same as we find in the report. Could you explain whether what the report says is right or whether we have to rely on what you tell us now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we have clarification as to what report you're referencing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I meant the letter where I said the report. But it has been reported that this was the reason given by Mr. Demurenko for his requests. In that sense it is a report as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer for opinions or interpretations of some colonels on the Serb side. They could have written whatever they pleased. I explained to you why I wanted to visit the Serbian territory. How they interpreted it and what they put in their document, I can't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you read it now. Are you telling us that it is not accurate what is in this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this letter is not in Russian. It's possible for me to miss important details. And, second, I don't want to be answerable for somebody else's letters. I answer only for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the text has been read to you and translated to you in Russian, but I leave it to that. We'll take a break first. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes; 5 minutes past 11.00, local time in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the videolink still functioning properly, sound and what you see?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the representative of the Registry confirm that the videolink is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, we can see and hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Tieger, please proceed. But before you do so, I take it that you read from a corrected translation which is apparently not in e-court yet and we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- give permission to replace the translation by the newly uploaded one and then to give the Defence an opportunity to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That has been done and there was an understanding between the parties that the new version would be uploaded. It's simply that that logistical aspect just wasn't completed. But the discussions took place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's under a -- yes, then the Registrar is hereby instructed to replace the existing translation of -- could you remind me of the number, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That the newly uploaded version replaces the old one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, before we leave this document, two hopefully quick matters. If we -- I just want to confirm that you were shown this document in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to 65 ter 33681, e-court page 25, which is transcript page 28965; it's in tab 17 of the Registrar's binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Can you repeat the transcript page number, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the correct page on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here in the middle of the page, Colonel, we see the discussion about the document being presented for your perusal, indicating this is a document issued by chief Colonel Marko Lugonja, et cetera. First, the discussion about information that you had disagreed with the assessment of UNPROFOR, proposed being given permission to visit the location which UNPROFOR assessed as the point from which the shell had been fired, also indicates that had you requested to visit hospitals in Blazuj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have that document enlarged, please, and it's not necessary to have it twice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then it continues: "I propose" -- with Colonel Lugonja continuing: "I propose to grant him permission for this too," et cetera. Turning the page in English now. And then, Colonel, if which look at -- toward the bottom of the next page 28966, e-court page 26 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I know there are technical problems. I just want to confirm that the -- okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked: "Q. Okay. So this document is then accurate in its confirmation that you sought and received permission to go to particular areas? "A. Yes, yes." And, Colonel, you can confirm that that was your testimony in the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't because the text in front of me is not in Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Based on --

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my experience from previous sessions is that my words were often replaced by different words -- by different words, so I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I tender these two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. Still to be uploaded in its extracted version, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit Number P7844, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, at least in the new version, only two pages. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, in addition, the request was made, the reply was received to that request, it was determined when it would be implemented, with whom, and a military guide was made available to assist you and your team in going to the location; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They always had to second a representative of one or the other side to accompany us into, for instance, a minefield or help us not get shelled or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in this instance, of course, the representative was from the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about that side of the front line, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd like to turn next to another portion of your statement. This located at paragraph 38 of your statement, which is, for the benefit of the parties, D02120. Paragraph 38 of your statement, Colonel, states the following: "The only incident between the Serb forces and the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo after the NATO bombing of the Serb positions that I remember was the fighting at the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge in Sarajevo. There were two check-points from both (Serb and Muslims) sides of the bridge and the Serbs and Muslims were shooting against each other. The Serb soldiers then went on an offensive and captured the Bosnian Muslim trenches. The Bosnian Muslims informed the French UNPROFOR about this and the French command ordered its French troops to attack the Serb units at the occupied check-point. The French soldiers attacked the Serbs and both French and Serb soldiers got killed in this attack. If I remember correctly, some seven French and ten Serb soldiers got killed in this fighting. It was a big scandal within the UN because the UN forces directly attacked one of the warring sides." Now, Colonel, during your testimony in the Karadzic case, I presented you with a code cable from General Janvier to Kofi Annan dated the 27th of May, 1995, which is P2559 in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could call up P2559, please. It's tab 12 of the Registry's binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look toward the bottom of the page under the item marked 4, we see the following report from Janvier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have it in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Starting at the second sentence of item 4: "At about 0430 hours this morning a group of BSA, Bosnian Serb army (assessed to be special forces), dressed in French UN uniforms and equipment, took over the FreBat 4 OP at Vrbanja bridge in Sarajevo and removed ten French soldiers. During the course of this action one French officer escaped. At 0800 hours FreBat 4 mounted a successful operation to regain control of the OP. As a result of this operation, one Bosnian Serb army soldier was killed and three are held by FreBat 4. Two French soldiers were killed (one not related to the operation to recover the OP) and two wounded (one seriously)." After I presented you with that document, Colonel, I asked you at page 28974 of the Karadzic transcript: "So, in fact, Colonel, it was not the case that the Muslims ran to UNPROFOR after their position was captured and then UNPROFOR went on the attack on their behalf. It was the case that the Bosnian Serbs attacked the French observation post wearing French uniforms and then the French Battalion retook the position. Isn't that correct? " And you answered: "No, no, that's not right. You took as evidence a report from the Superior Command, as I understand, a report by General Janvier to the UN." Now the next -- this continues on page 28975 of 65 ter 33681: "Why don't you take a sitrep that speaks to the same incident in Sector Sarajevo where it happened and compare the information in one report and the other. As you understand, on the ground things are much clearer than up at the top and then you would see what actually happened." Now, Colonel, can I take it that you agree that what I just read accurately reflects what was asked and what you answered on the 17th of October, 2012, during your testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the position --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak into the microphone, please, and all other microphones should be switched off. The witness has to start over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Witness, could you, first of all, speak into the microphone and could you again start your answer, or coming closer to where the microphone is located, and could you repeat what you said and finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It's good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, what you said is absolutely correct concerning the fact that there were perfectly correct descriptions below compared to the top. In one place there was a correct report on the victims and in other places something completely different. To be quite honest, I don't remember exactly what the report of General Janvier said about the -- the dressing in French uniforms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but it happened frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, one second. The only question Mr. Tieger asked you at this moment is whether what he read to you, whether that reflects what you testified in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not taking back a single word I said in previous trials. I talk about things that I remember. Whatever I remember, I'm prepared to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was read to you, you recognised that as the answers you gave in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A lot has been read back to me. Janvier's report, the sitreps, et cetera. Many of these things are mutually contradictory. Now I am hard put to say that to a comma and to a full stop everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was read to you by Mr. Tieger a second ago, the gist of that reflects what you remember to have testified in the Karadzic case. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I trust the materials of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I should -- in that case should probably tender the materials of the Court. That was page 28974 and 28975 of the Karadzic case which is 65 ter 33681, pages 34 through 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But 33681 has already been admitted, Mr. Tieger, as P7844.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another portion. Would it not be good that finally that you would upload all those pages you used from the Karadzic transcript and that we gather them together under that one number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I was going to suggest, Your Honours, since I believe that -- I believe counsel is going to add one more page at least with the following questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Colonel, let's follow up then on that response and your suggestion to look at a local sitrep, a sitrep from Sector Sarajevo and see what it says about the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that respect, can we call up 65 ter number 33674.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as can you see, Colonel, this is a sitrep of the same date, the 27th of May, 1995, referring on its very first page to the confrontation between the Bosnian Serb army and UNPROFOR with reconquest at the Vrbanja OP East, and that's in the fourth item down under "general assessments" on the first page. And as we see in the middle of the page, Colonel, the releasing officer on this sitrep from Sector Sarajevo is Colonel Demurenko, is you. Now, if we turn to page 4, please, we'll see further discussion of the event. On the second small paragraph under "assessment of impact, the hottest point was the reconquest of FreBat 4 of the Vrbanja bridge OP seized by trickery during the last night by Bosnian Serb army, dressed like UNPROFOR personnel with dead, wounded and captured personnel OP of both sides (two times dead and one time -- or 11 time injured French soldiers)." There's a further reference down there to orient you to the time, to the Bosnian Serb army keeping personnel like hostages especially the Ukrainian WCP in Ilidza. If we turn then to page 7, further discussion of this incident in the local sitrep which you suggested we look at. Here in the second listed item: "FreBat 4 at 27," meaning 27 May, "0400, Bosnian Serb soldiers invade the Vrbanja bridge OP dressed with UN equipment. Between 0800 and 0900, a platoon of FreBat 4 reconquered the OP accepted the OP western of the position (inside, there are eight Bosnian Serb army soldiers and one UNPROFOR soldier, French). One UNPROFOR soldier was killed and UNPROFOR soldiers were wounded. The FreBat 4 have four BSA prisoners." And finally turning to a couple of more pages, first page 10 and 11, where we can see the chronology of events from the 26th to the 27th, looking at the second item from the bottom: "Reports that today about 0430 Bosnian Serb army soldiers who were wearing in the UN French clothes (uniform, helmet, flakjacket) seized Vrbanja bridge and blocked 12 French UN soldiers in the OP." And if we turn to the next page looking at the fourth item down: "Vrbanja bridge OP East is reoccupied by French soldiers. One Bosnian Serb army soldier is killed and three injured. Three another Bosnian Serb army soldiers are seized as prisoners of FreBat 4. "One FreBat 4 soldier is killed and two soldiers injured." So, Colonel, contrary to your suggestion that if we looked at a local sitrep from Sector Sarajevo addressing this incident we would find that Janvier was wrong and the characterisation of events in your statement was correct, the truth is that the sitrep, the local sitrep, which was released by you on the date of the incident, confirms that the Bosnian Serbs using trickery attacked and took the French position and then the French retook the position a few hours later, not that the UN attacked after the Bosnian Muslims had been routed. That's the truth of the matter, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Why do you always take examples about Bosnian Serbs and you don't take examples of Bosniaks who used this trickery of changing into different clothes? That's one. Second, I am the author of the sitrep and I sign it, whereas the information is provided by other people and it's often wrong. The intelligence was, for instance, mainly US, and the information they provided was frequently not objective. And you keep citing examples of Bosnian Serbs and their trickery, whereas you can find equal examples of Bosniaks using the same trickery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 33674, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33674 receives Exhibit P7845, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let's turn next to 65 ter 33714, a document I know you're familiar with, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's in tab 21 of the Registrar's binder. It's a publication of Komsomolskaya Pravda entitled: The Bosnian confession of Colonel Demurenko. If you look at the very -- sorry, do you have it available now, Colonel? I see you do. Look at the top of the article, next to the picture at the top, it's the introduction to the remainder of that publication. It refers first to you, noting that there was one person who dared to doubt and that was peacekeeper Demurenko, that you conducted your own investigation. Next paragraph, it indicates your name again. Demurenko was declared a national hero by the Serbs, and then in the final sentence of that paragraph, it indicates this is very complicated when more and more trenches are needed by some and this is what Andrey Demurenko writes about his diaries, and then it contains various excerpts which I think you'll recall we discussed in the Karadzic -- some of which we discussed in the Karadzic case; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would be very grateful if counsel could turn off his microphone while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure we got your full answer, Colonel. I think you said: "Yes, I understand that." But if you said more, it might have been cut off when the interpreter was admonishing me to turn off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that articles about the former Yugoslav war were many. I remember that this correspondent took an interview with me, and I remember that an article was written. Yes, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And in particular, Colonel, if we turn to page 3 of the article in English, and for you, that would be found in the second column in approximately the middle of the page next to that insert to the right, you talked about the fact that it would be difficult to find a better commander than General Mladic. He is extremely talented, exceptionally literate, tough commander. You talked about the closeness between Russians and Serbs saying, "yes, these are people whom we consider very dear, we were brought together by history and there is no point in breaking these ties." You talked about General Mladic saying to your face that Russia had betrayed the Serbs, accusing Russia of betrayal, and explaining that "we would be happy to help our neighbours but that we were having trouble with our own ailments" and you were very embarrassed. And if we turn the page in English, we see a more casual reference to General Gobilliard's three-mile morning run along Sniper Alley. And during the course of your testimony in the Karadzic case, you confirmed the accuracy of the article's representations about your position. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 65 ter 33714, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P7846, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Tieger, where are we in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have -- well, we're close. I mean, I'm in my last -- now my last section which deals with one -- with one discrete issue which deals with two issues, but I would say I would be optimistic of completing that within ten minutes or so, ten to 15 minutes and no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we take the break first because it would be another extended session and that you have 15 more minutes after the break. We take a break. Mr. Demurenko, we'd like to see you back at five minutes past 12.00. Before we, however, leave the courtroom, Mr. Ivetic, could you give us an estimate of the time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Probably not more than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's clear. We will resume at five minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Expecting that Moscow can see and hear us, you're invited, Mr. Tieger, to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can I take up three housekeeping matters first. Number one, the excerpted photos from 65 ter 19792 have now been uploaded under 65 ter 1972b -- 19792b, and we would therefore ask that it be assigned P07843.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you check the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of the P number, Your Honour, or the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll recite it again as it's written, 19792b.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just check. Yes, it already has the number. It's now -- you have uploaded the selection of photographs which was admitted under this condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the condition is now fulfilled. Yes, next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And next is -- I realised I didn't tender 65 ter 1D03888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was? Which was, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Lugonja report or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D03888 receives Exhibit Number P7847, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's still an ongoing matter. There may be more, so I'll refrain from tendering that at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, earlier, that is, in June, you were asked at transcript page 44175 by His Honour Judge Moloto the following: "I have another question too. You've talked about taking photographs as you were walking along that distance. Do you have those photographs?" And you answered: "I handed them over at the last trial I attended. Of course, we made a huge number of photos, hundreds, but I supplied the most important ones, I think 10 or 20. I had brought them with me to prove my point." And then at the next page, at 44176 of the transcript of the 15th of June, you added: "I remember the Court," referring to the Karadzic Chamber, "had no doubts about the veracity of my testimony because the Court accepted the photographs." Then added you didn't know which party had tendered the photographs into evidence. I'd like to look, then, at a list of the exhibits that were tendered through you in the Karadzic case. That's 65 ter 33830. Now, there were approximately a total of -- we looked at -- last page -- 67 exhibits tendered during the course of your Karadzic testimony by the Defence or Prosecution, but the photographs are reflected on the first page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In items 4, 8, 9, and 10. And, unsurprisingly, those are the same photographs that were admitted in this case of you. So D2273 in Karadzic is D2140 here in this case admitted; 2277 is D2145; D2278 in Karadzic is D2144 here; and D2279 in Karadzic is D2146. And those four photographs which have now been tendered in the last two cases in which you testified depicting locations which you visited are the exact same number as the specific locations you identified in your press conference video, D2122, that you said you visited, pointing to -- with your pen to four separate locations on the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation line. That's the truth, isn't it, Colonel, that there are four photographs that were introduced by you in both cases, not ten or 20 or any other number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll object as it misstates the evidence. The portion of the transcript read by Mr. Tieger indicates that the witness gave 20 photographs to -- I believe he may have identified Marko from the Karadzic Defence. It does not specify the number that were admitted. He just says the Trial Chamber admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You know -- I have to interrupt. That's a speaking objection which is trying -- which has the purposeful or unintended effect of signalling items to the witness. We can take some time to discuss it but as I referenced --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, am I allowed to make my objection on the record. The section that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- he read from the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger was responding. You shouldn't interrupt him at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He cannot respond until I'm done giving the objection. I was still speaking, Your Honours. He interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, then I may have missed that. Your objection should be limited to not -- should be limited in the sense that it doesn't guide the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if need be, you can make objections while the witness takes his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, if we can go back to the section of the transcript -- if I go back to -- I'll just read Mr. Tieger's question, let's put it that way. At temporary transcript page 39, line 9, Mr. Tieger starts by saying: "Okay. Witness, earlier, that is, in June, you were asked at transcript page 44175 by His Honour Judge Moloto the following: "'I have another question too. You've talked about taking photographs as you were walking along the distance. Do you have those photographs?' "And you answered: "'I handed them over at the last trial I attended. Of course, we made a huge number of photos, hundreds, but I supplied the most important ones, I think 10 or'" -- it says 120, but I think it was 20 in the Karadzic transcript -- pardon me, in our transcript from June 15th. "'I had brought them with me to prove my point.'" Then Mr. Tieger goes on to the next page of the transcript of the 15th of June: "... you added: "'I remember the Court,' referring to the Karadzic Chamber, 'had no doubts about the veracity of my testimony because the Court accepted the photographs.'" He is not talking about all of the photographs he took. It's not identifying what number were accepted. So to say that this document now shows a different image than what the witness testified about is misstating the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to cut matters short. If the same number of photographs were tendered and admitted in Karadzic, and I take it that that's your position, just four, and if the same are admitted here, then the Chamber will be able to assess the probative value of the testimony of the witness that accepting such photographs means what the witness -- the meaning the witness attaches to that, because the situation then in Karadzic and the situation in this Chamber is exactly the same. Let's leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, the photographs are tendered because they were associated to the statement which is the Karadzic statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I say is if the witness gives a specific meaning of the Chamber accepting the photographs, which I do understand also on the basis of your submission, that is tendered and admitted, then we are exactly here in the same situation, and this Chamber is fully able to make up for itself on what it means that those four photographs are admitted into evidence as they were in the Karadzic case. I think it's -- there's not much more to be said about it. I don't know whether you insist on further asking questions about this to the witness, Mr. Tieger, because then [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we leave it to that. The question is put, objected to, and Mr. Tieger does not insist on an answer to his question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, finally, Colonel, in respect of your testimony to this Court that the Karadzic Chamber had no doubts about the veracity of your testimony, I'd like to look at, in fact, what the Trial Chamber considered about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that respect, I'd like 65 ter 33829, found at tab 22 of the Registrar's binder. This is paragraph 4342 of the Karadzic Judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning to the fourth sentence of that paragraph: "Thus, the Chamber did not find Demurenko credible when he testified that no suitable positions existed on the SRK side of the confrontation line nor did it believe him when he testified that he in fact examined an area much larger than the one he discussed in his interview of 2 September 1995 and in his evidence in the Dragomir Milosevic case. The Chamber considers that examining an area covering all of the directions of fire established at the time, together with the margin of error, would have been impossible in the limited amount of time Demurenko had. In addition, the Chamber finds it telling that he only mentioned this broader investigation [sic] after the Trial Chamber in the Dragomir Milosevic case" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It says "inspection" instead of "investigation," "this broader inspection after the Trial Chamber ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll repeat the sentence. "In addition, the Chamber finds it telling that he only mentioned this broader inspection after the Trial Chamber in the Dragomir Milosevic case had dismissed his investigation as having been too narrow. The Chamber is, therefore, convinced that Demurenko simply changed his testimony in order to counteract the findings of that Trial Chamber." The fact is, Colonel, that contrary to your claim to this Court that the Karadzic Trial Chamber found -- had no -- "had no doubts about the veracity" of your testimony, they considered that you were not credible; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm to take you at your word in your last sentence, namely, that the Court does not trust Witness Demurenko, then all my activity in my coming to this court to give evidence over the past few years is pointless. What was the point of listening to my arguments instead of just saying, No, you are wrong. This just shows your bias and lack of neutrality. You are biased and it was clear already at the last session when during the second day, the President of the Court repeated the questions of the Defence counsel three times and repeated your questions 13 times. That was clear pressure on the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are supposed not to comment on the behaviour of the parties or of this Chamber. You are here, again, not to hear your -- that we can hear your argument. We are here to listen to your testimony as a witness of fact. Would you please be so kind to answer the question. The question was about where you claimed that the other Trial Chamber by accepting your photographs thought that you gave reliable evidence, that this portion of the Judgement suggests or states that they were not convinced by the reliability of your evidence in this specific respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I'm answering the way I see it. I provided these photographs because they were needed at the moment. If the Chamber had asked me for more photographs, I have dozens, if not hundreds. Some of them I still keep. I would have provided the rest but they were not needed so they remained in my private archive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not exactly an answer to Mr. Tieger's question as I repeated it. But, Mr. Tieger, please proceed. But I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm mindful of the time, Mr. President, and I think at this point I would only tender the remaining portions of 65 ter 33681 that now is the -- the excerpt is from the Karadzic transcript. They've now been uploaded into e-court under 33681a and we'd ask that they be assigned P7844.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we note that transcript page 28964 of the Karadzic transcript dealing with the Lugonja document which has now been admitted into court is not included in the section that Mr. Tieger discussed the witness with [sic]. We would ask that that be included as well for context since that's where the questioning starts about that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you verify that, Mr. Tieger, apart from that it is mainly an administrative matter, to have uploaded the portions also Mr. Ivetic referred to. Take your time to verify. I mean, it's not an urgent matter. It's not -- no decision on admissibility in itself has to be taken. It is just an administrative follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, Mr. Ivetic will now re-examine you once he has installed the furniture. Mr. Ivetic, if you are ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, first of all, allow me to greet and welcome you back, since it has been such a long time. I, therefore, wish you a good day. The first questions that I want to ask you about is in relation to the multiple times in the transcript of the cross-examination when you were asked about your prior answers in the Dragomir Milosevic trial. Do you recall if, during the Dragomir Milosevic trial, your testimony was completely done with Russian translation or were there times when it was also conducted in English?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as here today, standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now I want to move to focus on the investigation of the Markale market incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you allow me to put one question --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- with respect to interpretation. Mr. Demurenko, do you remember if in the Karadzic case you testified also with interpretation or in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, 99 per cent of the time I speak Russian. Although there were a couple of sentences I said in English in those trials, but that was a mistake. I testified in Russian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to focus on the investigation that your team undertook as to the Markale market incident. You were asked several times about the video of your press conference that you gave in 1995, which has been admitted as, I believe, D2122 in those proceedings, and you were asked several times by the Prosecution and Trial Chamber as to the angle of descent and the issue of a line being drawn on a map. And we see this primarily from the transcript of the 15 June 2016 court date at transcript pages 44115 to 44116. And you repeatedly told both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber the same thing; namely that you relied on the results of the prior investigations for both the line on the map and the angle of descent. And we'll get to that, but I'd first like to ask you: After getting information from the prior investigations, what steps did your team take to determine what path you had to travel on the actual territory to conduct your investigation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was quite simple. We had a map and it was visible on the map. We only had to agree with the warring parties about the possibility for the group to travel that route, and we headed out with cameras and with the required good will to investigate properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you indicated you had the map. How did you use the map to identify the path that you had to travel through? Were there any steps taken before setting out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a military man, a professional, nothing much is needed. As I explained in the previous session, not even a GPS is needed. We can see on the spot the lie of the land. We mark landmarks and we follow the route uphill from one way point to another way point, following the route as indicated on the map, as charted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you say that you marked landmarks and you follow a route via way points. What devices or procedures are undertaken to identify landmarks and way points?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we had no GPS. We used the artillery compass and basic equipment, and that was enough to make a plan and chart a route.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now to focus on the interview, that is to say, the press conference that you gave in 1995, you were asked about -- by the Judge about why you did things the way you did in that press conference. And at transcript 44126, you said you were not a PR specialist and had no preparation for talking to the media. And I want to ask you: How much time did you have to prepare before giving that press conference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly to an hour but I had not more than one or two days to prepare. I had my bullet points and the photographs that I showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, several times during the cross-examination back in June, Mr. Tieger focused on the documents that you held in your hand during that interview, during that press conference. And he showed you 65 ter number 14297a and that is now in evidence as P7841 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then in the cross-examination, Mr. Tieger further showed you another document which he said showed that the UN investigation got 160 degrees and the other document that he showed you was P797, page 7, but he did not go through some other parts of that document or other documents with you. Now, at the transcript at page 44082, that's the part of the video of the press conference, when talking about the French report you say as follows: "No, the main serious facts for us is following. This is a material, maybe one portion of the whole material of UN specialist about the shelling. This is a short report with, is centred on French language but with strange conclusion." And then the press conference goes on. Now, based on what you recall, beyond this French report did you have access to other material from UN specialists in relation to Markale?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, I could have perhaps asked for other documents, but it was simply not necessary. All the UN experts were part of the contingent that was subordinate to me. It was enough for me to listen to the press conference that was falsely given by one representative, then to look at the drawings and sketches and maps showing trajectories and alternative trajectories, and then what remained was to assemble a group, get agreements from the two sides, and proceed with the investigation. It was rather a simple matter for a professional military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And during your press conference you referred to a photo, and it is 65 ter number 33705 on the Prosecution's list, which you should have there, so if you would like to take a look at it, but it's a photo you showed. And at transcript page 44083, lines 2 through 6, again, this is transcript from your press conference, you say as follows: "This is a picture about, it's very interesting, this material of Bosnian police, I mean, I mean, government Bosnian police, is about angle between ground and shell. As you can see degrees, and the last paper is really" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I see on the transcript 70 degrees, as you can see 70 degrees and I missed that in your reading, the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I must have ... yeah, that's correct. You are correct, Your Honours, I must have skipped over that in my reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you re-start then. It's about angle and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... is about, about angle between ground and shell. As can you see 70 degrees, and the last paper is really, this is a small slice of copy from map, and this is my idea which I can explain on this paper."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
