utterances.text: And then at this point of the press conference you started to draw with a free hand on paper to illustrate your investigation. And I want to ask you: Apart from this photo that you had in your hand from the Bosnian police, did you or members of your team perhaps consult other parts of the report of the Bosnian police as to the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, we had two pieces of paper in our hands. One was an excerpt from the map indicating possible trajectories; and the second was a drawing indicating the shell as it was landing at a certain angle --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Extra microphones must be turned off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm repeating. I had two pieces of paper in my hand. One of them was a diagram showing the shell and the angle of impact and also some numbers; and the second was an excerpt of the map showing two possible directions of descent. That was enough for any professional to search for possible positions where it was fired from, which we proceeded to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I didn't mind what the witness said in answer to your question. I leave it to that, but apparently you're satisfied with it. Yes, please proceed. For the record ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, P797, which Mr. Tieger used in cross-examination, at page 3 identifies 170 degrees as being found by the UNMO team. P2608, page 36 in Serbian and page 20 in the English similarly identifies 170 degrees, not the 160 Mr. Tieger was making reference to. And P496, page 2 in English and page 3 in the B/C/S, is the report of the official Bosnian police which says 170 degrees plus or minus 5 degrees, which again is not the 160 that Mr. Tieger was referencing during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, apparently this seems to be the beginning of argument, but could you please briefly respond on a factual -- 160 degrees --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just rising to make the same point. This is not appropriate for cross-examination. This the commencement of argument which will eventually take place but is not about the cross-examination I conducted or the steps taken by this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, when I made that same objection to the Prosecution doing this very same thing, I was struck down. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not going to further argue. You are referring to the 160 Mr. Tieger used. If you could, not necessarily now immediately, give us the exact transcript page where we find that. And again you can continue now to start with, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, I can continue and I'll get back to that. I think -- actually I can tell you right away. It was transcript page 44190 of the Mladic -- 44190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, anything to add at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't think such clarification was necessary but maybe it was. My point was -- arose out of the documents that we can see visible in the video, on the documents the witness indicated he had, and trying to decipher what was written on those documents and that was it. It is not a further argument about what happened in relation to the investigation more generally that didn't have to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it's clear what Mr. Ivetic was referring to. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I would now like to return to the map that you held in your hand with a line drawn on it. It's visible at 4 minutes and 14 seconds of the press conference video. Who drew the line on that map, was it your team or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. That was precisely why it was valuable to get a document from an interested party, such as the map and the trajectory of the shell, specifically so that later on, they could not say that the Russians or the Serbs or the UN or whoever deliberately made a sketch and conducted an investigation for themselves. We took as a basis a document made by the other side, started investigating and showed: you are cheating.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus on that bearing line that you went into the field to review based upon the map, you repeatedly told the Prosecution in cross-examination that you went along the whole line and not just points of the line. And so I want to ask you a question. If a 120-millimetre mortar had been fired by anyone along or near to that bearing line that you followed, what type of traces would you have expected to see evidencing such a mortar as being fired?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that question before but I will answer it again with pleasure. A mortar cannot be suspended in air. It has to rely on something and has to leave traces. There always - and I repeat always - remain traces of the use of land to place a mortar and to fire it, and there remain boxes lying around and cases of ammunition, et cetera. Nobody cleans up a place after using a mortar. It's not a public park. Either it was true and it had to be accepted that the Serbs were the aggressors or one had to inspect the possible places of firing and to prove otherwise, and then it was up to the UN to investigate further who actually fired the shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now during cross-examination, the Prosecution kept asking you about different types of 120-millimetre mortars and different types of 120-millimetre mortar shells. Do -- strike that. Are there any differences in the traces that you would expect to be found depending on the type of shell that was fired from a 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer that. The consultants that advised Mr. Tieger did a very bad job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, there were 120-millimetre mortars and shells of the same calibre provided by the Yugoslav army, but that is completely irrelevant. In any case, traces remain. They cannot evaporate, vanish into thin air. Some kind of trace always remain. They told us to look for 120-millimetre mortar shells or traces of a 120-millimetre mortar. We didn't find any, which means that there was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, again no answer to the question, but if you are satisfied, please go on. The question was whether the different types of 120-millimetre mortar shells leave different traces, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the answer then at line 11: "In any case, traces remain."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, if that's an -- if you consider that to be an answer, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me then ask a follow-up question to address Your Honours' concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does the existence of a trace on the ground from a fired mortar matter -- pardon me. Does the type of round used in a mortar matter in relation to the existence of a trace on the ground from the firing of that mortar?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in order to understand whether something was fired or not, it doesn't make any difference. But if you put the question differently. We know that something was fired. You, the investigators, find out which type of mortar and which type of ammunition was used. Then we would use different equipment to find out what kind of cases are left, to establish diameters of traces, et cetera. We would do it differently. But that question was not put. The question was whether a mortar was fired from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to that question of whether a mortar was fired from there, does the type of shell used make any difference as to the existence of traces on the ground from that firing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely none. Any mortar shell, modified or old 120 millimetre or other, leaves the same kind of traces. And the same shrapnel and the same crater.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to the questions posed to you today as to paragraph 38 of your 92 ter statement, D2120, and it will be on page 13 of the document. I will read it to you since I thought I heard that the -- that that page was missing from the materials that were sent there. And this is -- this the statement talking about the incident between the French UNPROFOR and the Serbs, and it says: "The only incident between the Serb forces and the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo after the NATO bombing of the Serb positions that I remember was the fighting at the Brotherhood and Unity bridge in Sarajevo. There were two check-points from both (Serb and Muslims) sides of the bridge and the Serbs and Muslims were shooting against each other. The Serb soldiers then went on an offensive and captured the Bosnian Muslim trenches. The Bosnian Muslims informed the French UNPROFOR about this and the French command ordered its French troops to attack the Serb units at the occupied check-point. The French soldiers attacked the Serbs and both French and Serb soldiers got killed in this attack. If I remember correctly, some seven French and ten Serb soldiers got killed in this fighting. It was a big scandal within the UN because the UN forces directly attacked one of the warring sides." And the first question I have for you is: What is the basis or source for the information that you have relayed in this paragraph of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all in the reports, all types of reports, because they were made not only by intelligence units but also all the contingents of the UN, all the check-points, all the military observers, et cetera. So several times a day, we received reports on the situation in the sector, and as soon as that happened at the Brotherhood and Unity bridge, I found out about it and I headed out to see with my own eyes what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated you wanted to see with your own eyes what had happened. Were you able to, in fact, see with your own eyes any part of these activities that are relayed in paragraph 38?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did see was the place, the results of the tragedy that had taken place, the blood on the tarmac. The wounded and the killed had been taken away by that time, but they were already in hospitals, and I regularly visited hospitals for moral support. I had been at that bridge many times, and after the incident, I simply went out on purpose to see the aftermath of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- additional question in this respect. When you went to that place, did you see an observation post which, I think it was number 4, FreBat number 4, there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I saw the observation point on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking for specifically this observation point from FreBat 4 which appears in the report you signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the observation point of the French Battalion. Now, the name of the battalion and the number of the observation post I can't tell you now because I had seen thousands. It was not my purpose at that time to establish this type of detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that where you saw the blood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The blood-stains were around the Bosnian check-point and the Serbian check-point, where the fighting had taken place using automatic weapons, where the killed and the wounded had spilt their blood on the tarmac. That has nothing to do with the observation point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you describe in paragraph 38, then, of your statement is not the same event as was in the reports we have looked at about FreBat 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Several times Mr. Tieger referred to some problems in Blazuj, in some other locations in Sarajevo. It all got blended together and confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, my question is not blending anything together. What I was asking you is that the re-taking of a certain position by the French UNPROFOR, whether they re-took both their own observation post and a check-point or whether it's all one event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember well, the Serbian troops did not take any observation points. That was a war between two parties, the Bosniaks and the Serbs. The Serbs did not set themselves the task of capturing an observation post. The Bosnians attacked, and the French tried to repel the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, not an answer to my question. But, Mr. Ivetic, if you wish to proceed, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to figure out how to proceed, Your Honour, but Your Honour has asked two questions that I don't see being the same questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there's no need to comment on my questions. If you have any questions to be put to the witness, you may put them to the witness, and the thinking is not necessarily done aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can take a look at what was 65 ter number 33674 used with you today and therefore it should be there in the packet that the Prosecution provided. It has now been admitted into evidence as P7845 or 95, I can't read my own handwriting, but this was the -- there it is on the screen right now. I believe this is what --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -45, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe this is the report that Judge Orie was asking about as to FreBat 4. And the question that I would ask in follow up is: Do you know if this incident which is said to take place at the Vrbanja bridge is the same incident that you describe in paragraph 38 of your statement as being at the Brotherhood and Unity bridge. Do you know if they're one and the same or what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you starting from that? First of all, we can look at the times. 27 May was the date of the incident in Vrbanja, and at the Brotherhood and Unity bridge the incident was in September, and these are two different places rather far, one from another.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank, you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now for my last several questions, I actually need the guidance of Your Honours. At the beginning of today the witness waived confidentiality for a certain document, from the memorandum, and I have some questions to pose as to that memorandum. The Defence position always has been that the memorandum with the names of the VWS personnel redacted should be public, I think we've made that clear in our various filings, and therefore we believe the questions posed about that memorandum, excerpting the names the VWS personnel, should be made in public. But Your Honours gave a date of 22nd August for both parties to provide any objections to any parts of that being made public, and so I don't know whether I should proceed now in open session or otherwise, and I ask Your Honours' instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, of course, the time is not there yet when you're supposed to make submissions. Reference to the memorandum, certainly without giving names of VWS officials, would that be opposed by the Prosecution to do that in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you cautiously use that memorandum, then there is no problem. But before you would do so, I have one question to the witness. Witness, you have read the memorandum shown to you earlier where you waived your right to confidentiality of your document. Yes, you are showing it to us. You also wrote us a letter. Now, do we have to primarily rely on the letter or do we have to primarily rely on the content of the memorandum in which VWS refers to communications with you? Which of the two gives the reasons? Because they're not the same, as you may have noticed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Naturally, please rely on my letter because the memorandum does not reflect the whole truth. I can comment further if you give me the possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say the memorandum does not give the whole truth, do I have to understand that at least what is said in the memorandum, that is, you being unhappy and perhaps even slightly irritated or strongly irritated by what happened to you on the 15th of June and perhaps the preceding day or days, that that still stands although is not the whole of the story. Is that how we have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to stress that the emphasis in the memorandum is on my emotional outbursts and dissatisfaction. You can ignore that. You can set that aside. That's not important. What is important is literally the last sentence, when you told me that it was necessary to continue the session the next day, and I told you that I had no time. And if you remember, the initial letter was I was able to attend from the 10th and the 16th -- until the 16th. To which you answered: It's your problem. You did not want to listen to me and you ignored my problem. That was the point, and I described all that in the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now one final question. You say your emotional response is not relevant. We can ignore that. But I would like to know is what is described there, whether that is what you communicated with VWS, the Victims and Witness Section, irrespective of how relevant that is? Does it reflect the content of your communication with the Victims and Witness Section?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reflects it truthfully. However, the secondary points were made in front of the most important ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, most importantly, that I could not stay the night because the next day I had to be at work. They did not, in other words, include in the memorandum what I said first. They included instead things that I had to say of the second order, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And on the 15th of -- you did not tell us, the Chamber, when we adjourned for the day and told you that we'd like to see you back the next morning on the 16th, you didn't tell us at that point in time that you couldn't come because you had to return to work. Is that your recollection as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember only that you did not let me say it. I was raising my hand, wanted to ask three questions. I could ask two and I couldn't ask the third. You didn't let me express my point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said immediately when they addressed me that I am going to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed, I'm also looking at the clock. How much time you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can't do it in two minutes, so why don't we take the break and we'll just have a short last session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have a few other matters to deal with as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so if we could -- if there's any chance that we could continue until 2.30, then that might be -- if you are short, and, Mr. Tieger, how much time would you need in --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Five minutes at most, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we're good with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Yes, but you don't know what we have on our agenda until 2.00. Madam Registrar, could you try to find out whether we could have a little bit of an extended session, and, Mr. Ivetic, could you discuss with your client whether we have to come back tomorrow or whether we could finalise it even if we go a little bit over the usual time. Then we'll take the break first, and how many more minutes you said you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would anticipate five to seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break first. We'll take the break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Expecting that the videolink is functioning well, Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to highlight various portions of this memorandum and I hope you have it in front of you in the Russian language. Unfortunately, I only have the English and therefore will have to read the English version. And again, we should not mention any of the names of the people that are identified in the memorandum. But I'd like to look at the third paragraph of this memorandum, which I will read in full and then ask some questions about, and it says: "Shortly thereafter," and then a name which we will not repeat, "visited the witness at the hotel and informed him that his testimony was not finished and that he had been orally instructed by the Trial Chamber to appear the next day at 9.30. She also advised him that the Trial Chamber could possibly hold him in contempt or at least subpoena him to complete his evidence. Upon her return to the office," again we won't mention the person's name, "informed VWS that the witness expressed the words to this effect that he felt under pressure and treated in an aggressive and unreasonable way, that he was insulted that he was not allowed to shake hands with General Mladic, and that he was not going to continue his testimony, that he had to return for his work and that he planned to make his own way to the airport and depart Holland, if necessary." And I think you've already answered to Judge Orie that everything here is true, just that the order is not accurate. Is everything here complete in terms of the information that you gave to the VRS -- to the VWS personnel on the 15th of June, 2016, or is something missing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the truth. It's only that the stresses are wrong, in the wrong places. In the first place was my need to return within the time-frame indicated in the letter that had been sent earlier from Moscow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to that letter, was that a letter sent by your employer or by yourself; and to whom?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was that with VWS or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean did someone else help me write the letter? No. I wrote it myself from Moscow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm saying that was the letter to VWS that you're talking about. Is that the letter we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, it was addressed to (redacted) - the woman who --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We shouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- had been in touch with me before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to be very careful here, Witness. Is that -- the letter that you're referring to, is that the letter sent to the Victims and Witness Section and, as the Chamber understood, as letter of the same content to the Defence? That is the letter you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like us to talk about one and the same letter. I don't know her official position or title, but it's the woman who had been keeping in touch with me before I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now in this paragraph, it is indicated here that you "felt under pressure and treated in an aggressive and unreasonable way." By whom did you feel pressured and treated aggressively and in an unreasonable way?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I refrain from answering that question? I would not like to create any more discomfort for the esteemed personnel of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll ask you, earlier you indicated you had -- you wanted to make some comments or commentary as to this memorandum, and I'd like to give you the opportunity now to identify any other comments that you have about the content of this memorandum, but cautioning that you should not identify the names of any of the individuals that are mentioned in it from the VS service.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did express my position in bits and pieces already. Going up to the first paragraph, the questions and answers in the first session. Then referring to the confidential part. There's the issue of my employer and his requirements. The fact that the session was first scheduled for the 13th, then was delayed until the 14th, then was postponed until the 15th. And eventually my employer decided to accommodate only me personally and gave me permission to stay away until the 16th. I have nothing to add, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. Then, in that case, I only would thank you again on behalf of myself personally and my client and the rest of the team for all of your testimony and for agreeing to come back via videolink to complete it. We thank you and appreciate it and apologise for any inconvenience that you may have felt from the Defence side, if there was any. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, my only remaining question concerns page 38 of your statement, that portion of the statement that deals with the incident on the bridge. Earlier today you'll recall that in connection with that, I pointed out your testimony in the Karadzic case during which the Janvier report was shown to you - that report is 2559 in this case - and read out to you what you said at the time in response to being shown that document and what you said to this -- and it's now in evidence -- that transcript is going to be in evidence. You pointed out that -- or why -- you asked: "Why don't you take a sitrep that speaks to the same incident in Sector Sarajevo where it happened and compare the information in one report and the other. As you understand, on the ground things are much clearer than up at the top and then you would see what exactly happened?" And then we continued during the course of your examination today to call up your sitrep or the sitrep you released from the 27th of May and discussed that, but what we didn't do -- I would now like to turn to what you said in the Karadzic case when you were confronted with the same document. And that's found at transcript page 28975 of the Karadzic testimony, which is 65 ter 33681 at page 35. That should be one of the pages -- the last page uploaded under -- or one of the pages uploaded under 33681a already. And so after your invitation to take a sitrep that speaks to the same incident in Sector Sarajevo, we called this document up in the Karadzic case. We looked at it here today. Here's what you said in -- so you were asked about that, and as we can see from this portion of the transcript and the question, you had a chance to see the same references in that document that you saw here today: The reference on the first page; the references on page 4 about the hottest point was the reconquest by FreBat 4 of the Vrbanja bridge; the reference on page 7, Bosnian Serb army soldiers invade the Vrbanja bridge dressed in UN equipment. And then the references in the chronology on pages 10 and 11 of the document reflecting that at 0430 Bosnian Serb army soldiers who were wearing the UN French clothes, et cetera, seized the bridge, blocked the soldiers, and then the reference on the next page to the retaking of that. And when presented with that document in the Karadzic case, you said the following, Colonel, and that's found on the next page, 28976: "It would be advantageous for me to use your methods when you compared the figures, the figures that I mentioned and the figures that you had had in your hands. If we were to have a bit more time, which we don't have, and if we were to look at the first report where it said 4.30 in the morning, nine soldiers, ten soldiers, and then they mention the uniform of the special forces of the French army, whereas in this document they mention the UN uniforms, not the French uniforms. So there's a lot of contradiction in these three reports. This is just another indication of the manipulation that took place. Depending on who signed the report, they twisted the truth, they twisted the reality, put their spin on it. So in all these three documents that you showed, the time, the participants, the uniforms, all of that is described differently. That means that one could play it any way one wanted, relying on each of these reports individually." So when presented with your sitrep in the -- from 27th of May, when presented with that document in the Karadzic case, you did not assert that this represented a different incident than the one referred to in paragraph 38 of your report. You said, just as you had said about the Janvier report, that it can't be trusted because of the alleged contradictions, about the uniform and the number of persons killed and so on, between your sitrep and the Janvier report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will object because the section that has been quoted also says at line 5: "If we were to have a bit more time, which we don't have," and then talks about what they could find looking through the documents. So I don't believe that it's fair to say that this is a complete analysis or rendition of the various documents that were shown to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear Mr. Tieger presenting it as a complete analysis. He just put, I think, to the witness what he found in the testimony, and indeed the words you apparently considered to be of importance have now been added. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's essentially correct, isn't it, Colonel, that what you said was that the alleged discrepancies between the description of the event in your sitrep and the Janvier report indicated that it couldn't be trusted, but you never suggested that, in fact, the Janvier report and your 27 May sitrep were referring to different events than the one described in your statement in paragraph 38?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is too much background noise. The interpreter can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Karadzic case and were shown the same documents you saw here today, you said that the Janvier report and your own sitrep, the sitrep you released yourself on the 27th of May, simply couldn't be trusted about what happened on that date because of the alleged discrepancies that you referred to, but you didn't suggest, much less -- you didn't say, much less suggest, that these -- that the Janvier report and the 27 May sitrep referred to a different event than the one described in paragraph 38 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew your attention to the fact that these were two different sitreps and two different locations. Vrbanja and the bridge -- and the other bridge are two different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You also --

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is never a 100 per cent coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll just add, if I may, add that to the Karadzic excerpts and leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. How far away are the two bridges from another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. One other question. You said you went to the place of the incident. That's where you saw the FreBat 4 observation post. Where was that bridge located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Brotherhood and Unity bridge used to be at least across the Miljacka river in the centre of the city, approximately, near the memorial plaque saying that it was a site where Gavrilo Princip had killed Crown Prince Ferdinand. And I just walked across that bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when you visited the site of the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, within two hours of the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the incident took place two hours away from the centre of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said two hours within -- within two hours from the incident and the -- the bridge is in the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think for the sake of completeness, if I may have just one more reference to refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will try to. If we could turn to page 32 of 33681, and we -- this will complete the entire colloquy during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in the Karadzic case you were asked the following, starting at the bottom, actually, of page 28972, that's page 32, as follows: "Colonel, you discussed an incident that you asserted took place at -- you discussed was what you called the only incident between Serb forces and UNPROFOR after the NATO bombing, and that was what you said to be the fighting at the Brotherhood and Unity bridge. That's at your amalgamated witness statement at paragraph 38. Would it refresh your recollection about where that incident took place if I told you that the only incident that took place between Serb forces and UNPROFOR after the NATO bombing was -- took place at the Vrbanja bridge. Is that the -- was that the incident you were discussing? "A. To be quite honest, I don't remember if the Brotherhood Unity bridge is the same as Vrbanja bridge or it's a different bridge. I simply don't remember. But I remember that on the Brotherhood and Unity bridge there was a lot of bloodshed in a mutual attack when many UNPROFOR soldiers, French soldiers, were killed, and there must have been other cases. I do remember. They did happen." And then we went on to discuss the documents we referred to earlier. Is that an accurate reflection of what you said in the Karadzic case as far as you recall, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This only goes to show that I'm not an automaton. I may have said that the Brotherhood and Unity bridge in my mind is not the same as Vrbanja, but it was in any case at totally different times. One was in May and another was in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then, with that, I thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would add those pages to 7844 and tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They will be included in the still-to-be-uploaded portions of the testimony. Mr. Demurenko, we are at the conclusion of hearing your evidence. I would like to express that we were glad that you could conclude your testimony, and I wish you a safe return home, even if it's not as far as it was before. Thank you very much. We can conclude the videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Would you allow me to add something? To thank everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Thank you. We'll now conclude the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd move on with a few procedural items I still have on my agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd first like to deliver the Chamber's decision on the Defence supplemental submission to admit the evidence of Jasmin Odobasic dated the 1st of August, 2016. On the 17th of June, 2016, the parties filed a joint motion pursuant to Rule 92 quater of the Rules tendering the written statement of Odobasic and related documents. The parties indicated that they would make a supplemental submission tendering excerpts of a book authored by the witness. On the 28 of July, the Chamber deferred its decision on the tendering of these excerpts as the parties had not yet agreed on which excerpts were to be tendered. On the 1st of August, the Defence filed a supplemental submission tendering into evidence the excerpts agreed between the parties which were uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter number 1D05976. The Chamber recalls the applicable law for the admission of evidence is as set out in Rule 89(C) of the Rules, which allows a Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. The Chamber has reviewed the proposed exhibit in light of Odobasic's statement and, although the witness did not specifically refer to the book in his statement, the Chamber considers it appropriate to have the proposed exhibit tendered through him as the subject matter of the book is sufficiently related to the witness's statement. With regard to relevance and probative value, the Chamber finds that the proposed exhibit contains information about exhumations throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and is therefore relevant to crimes charged in the indictment. The Chamber observes that the proposed exhibit contains information regarding its author and its publication and therefore considers that it bears sufficient indicia of reliability and authenticity for the purpose of admission into evidence. In light of the foregoing and pursuant to Rule 89(C) of the Rules, the Chamber grants the motion and admits the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D05976 into evidence. Madam Registrar, could you assign an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is D2180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D2180 is admitted into evidence, and this concludes the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move to item in relation to Exhibit D2035 which was on the 8th of June, 2016, admitted by the Chamber and the Chamber instructed the Defence to upload into e-court an English translation that corresponds to its B/C/S original. On the 4th of August, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution, via an e-mail, that the revised translation had been uploaded under doc ID 1D31-1538. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the existing translation of Exhibit D2035 with the revised one. The Prosecution has one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. Next item deals with Exhibit D2132. On the 26th of July, the Chamber admitted Exhibit D2132 into evidence. On the 3rd of August, the Defence e-mailed the Registry, the Chamber, and the Prosecution advising that the revised English translation of the exhibit had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 1D31-1588. The Chamber instructs the Registry the replace the current English translation of the exhibit with the revised one. The Prosecution has one week to revisit the matter, if necessary. I now come to my final issue. The Chamber recalls that Mr. Demurenko was the last witness to testify during the Defence case. Furthermore, during the last Status Conference on the 8th of July of this year, the Defence listed outstanding evidentiary motions, all of which would be filed within two weeks. The Chamber understands from all of this that the Defence has rested its case. And, Mr. Lukic, can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invited Mr. Lukic to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, if you allow Mr. Ivetic to respond. He is more privy with these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have a confidential decision that Your Honours issued yesterday in relation to two individuals which we will be filing a motion seeks certification to appeal. And we have filed a public motion on the 8th of August in relation to documents that were excerpted from the witness statement of Amor Masovic and admitted by this Chamber upon application by the Prosecution as bar table documents which we believe to be improper under the recently recited criteria that the Chamber has used to deny the Defence the ability to do likewise with documents that are not from witness statements, and therefore, in that motion we have sought for those documents to be stricken or, in the alternative, for the individual in question, Amor Masovic, to be called as a witness. And so subject to those three witnesses, Your Honours, the Defence does not rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say "does not rest," Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does not rest. We don't consider those matters to be closed yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do they have any suspensive effect on the presentation of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Three witnesses which we believe still should be heard, yes, Your Honours. Therefore we cannot rest until those matters are fully litigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if the Chamber would - I'm not saying it will - but if the Chamber would deny that, then there's nothing remaining, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And at that time then we would be able to reconsider this issue. But as I stand here now, I cannot rest because there are matters still pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, a motion for certification is the next step -- and the decision about certification to appeal is a step to be taken after the decision by the Chamber is filed. Therefore, it's not -- no longer part of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, I repeat: On August 8th, 2016, we filed a motion for which this Chamber has not issued a decision, so, therefore, I do believe it is part of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the motion dealing with systematic bias, is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dealing with Amor Masovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, Masovic. The Defence in the Masovic filing seeks reconsideration of a decision admitting charts into evidence during the Prosecution's case, and in the alternative, Masovic's testimony is sought, but it is not sought as part of the Defence case. It's not presentation of evidence by the Defence, and, therefore, in view of that, it has no impact on closing. As a matter of fact, you're suggesting what we are supposed to do or what the Prosecution should do, but it's not announcing what the Defence wishes to present as evidence. That's as far as Masovic is concerned. The others you're referring to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the confidential decision yesterday as to two individuals. That's -- it's the -- Your Honours had -- had denied a motion that had been filed upon the suggestion of the Honourable Judge Moloto at the Status Conference that we had in relation to two witnesses that we wanted to still call that were on our witness list, and that decision said that although they had not been removed from the witness list, the Defence could not call them. And that's the decision that we will be doing a certification to appeal. Those two witnesses are foreseen as being part of the Defence case, were indeed on our list, and as I understand it, we have not exhausted the time granted by Chamber for presentation of our Defence case. And, therefore, we believe that those two witnesses are definitely within the bounds of our Defence case. And again, it was a confidential decision, otherwise I would gladly tell you their names. If needed, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment we only have a request for issuing a certification to appeal, isn't it? Or not? Or not yet. You intend to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not yet. Your Honours filed the decision -- late yesterday we received it, so I don't know when it was drafted, but we got it late yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But it was decided upon yesterday and that means at the moment that your motion found a final decision, and if you now ask for certification to appeal, that is the next step beyond the resting of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, we also asked for reconsideration which would be within the bounds of this Chamber, not to the Appellate Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For those two, it was not decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have filed the decision yesterday and we now hear what plans the Defence still has.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it may join some of the other certification motions which are still pending and which have no suspensive effect, if it will be filed. All those certification motions, including one which may come but we're not aware of yet, are evidentiary. Certification or reconsideration motions do not have a suspensive effect and therefore do not impact on any closure of the case. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is one other matter which is D2177. The Prosecution, I think, responded that it would oppose reconsideration or a certificate to appeal but would not oppose tendering the whole of the document where the Chamber admitted only four pages until now, that it was about the positions taken by Russia and the witness testifying on whether he agreed with those positions, yes or no. I also do understand that the Defence in its motion gave as a final alternative to have the whole of D2177 to be admitted into evidence. The Chamber is inclined to follow the suggestion by the parties; that is, that D2177 will be admitted from the bar table and -- in its entirety. Any comment on what the Chamber ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have correctly stated the positions. I have just one procedural question. Since you had already instructed us to upload a redacted version which -- pardon me, a reduced version, can we upload the full version in the same 65 ter number or do we need to do anything different? That's the question I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was marked for identification as D2177. If you would upload the complete version of that document, then the Registry is hereby instructed to replace the present version of D2177 by the complete version of the same document. Mr. Tieger, you are looking as if something bothers you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just logistical, we thought that the entirety already existed under -- uploaded under a number, but one way or another that can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It does, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the entire document is already uploaded --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The original document was the entire -- you had asked for a reduced portion which had been uploaded and I don't -- I'm not sure if it had been replaced yet or not. That's why I wanted to make sure we didn't leave it hanging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, there is nothing to be replaced. I withdraw now the instruction to upload a four-page extract of that document. And D2177, as it is uploaded now into e-court, is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under these circumstances, no evidentiary issues remaining, the Chamber establishes that the Defence rests its case and that the Defence case is closed, with the caveat of the -- no, I think I leave it to that. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll move on. The Chamber further considers that it is in the interests of an expeditious completion of the evidentiary stage of this case to already receive any submissions pursuant to Rule 85 (A)(vi) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence tendering into evidence information relevant to determining an appropriate sentence if the accused is found guilty and orders the parties to make any submissions by the 25th of August, 2016. Lastly, I address the Prosecution. The Prosecution filed its rebuttal motion on the 21st of June, 2016. Not much Defence evidence has been admitted since, but I wanted to verify that there's no need for the Prosecution to supplement its rebuttal filing or is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then hereby verified. I have no further items on my agenda. Any matter to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, a strict housekeeping matter that Ms. Stewart advises me of. We didn't complete the tendering of P7844. All of the excerpts are now uploaded and those are T 28964 through 66 and T 28972 through 76 of the Karadzic transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Uploaded under what number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, all the -- only the pages dealt with with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the one that I added that was -- yeah, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is included as well. Madam Registrar, could you please assign a number to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think number -- it's P7844.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, the number is -- yes, the number was already reserved. P7844, which now covers the document uploaded under number 33681a, is admitted into evidence. Any other matter, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Only to mention that Prosecution also has an interest, as I think everyone in the courtroom does, in the most efficient and expeditious resolution of the case. We will continue to consider any steps including meeting with the Defence that may facilitate that, and in that connection would be prepared, I think, to seek from the Court periodic Status Conferences, even of relatively short duration, in the interests of moving matters forward and keeping the parties abreast of the status and any additional steps that could usefully be undertaken. So I'm not suggesting a specific date at the moment, but I think that foreshadowing that possibility even on a semi-regular basis is -- could be a useful method to move us forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates you -- your position. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have one issue we would like to stress to the Chamber. We have a motion seeking additional time for the final brief deadline which Your Honours had deferred ruling upon, and so maybe it's something you already had in mind, but I just want to make sure that that was still out there and that we do need a decision on that, to make sure that that wasn't left lost in the clutter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not lost, but we did not want to anticipate too much on what still could happen and now are in a better decision to decide on that motion, and we'll do that within due course. Any other matter to be raised? Then I didn't hear anything yet about roads and distances. I looked at it again, and I saw that one of the issues might be whether there's any macadam roads within 6 kilometres or there are no macadam roads within 6 kilometres from the point of impact. That perhaps gives a bit of more precise description of apparently what the Chamber encourages the parties to agree upon. If there is nothing left, most likely we will not see each other very soon again, we adjourn sine die.

procedural_notes.text: [The witness takes the stand via videolink]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.26 p.m.,
